title: The Weirdest Crusades in History
description:
A crusade that left months early, a crowd that waited for the sea to dry up, a friar who walked over to the sultan, an enemy who sent fruit and snow, a kidnapped king, an emperor who won Jerusalem with talks while excommunicated, and a crusade that attacked the wrong city. Here are the weirdest crusades in history, counted down from seven to one. Chapters are added automatically.

#history #crusades #medieval #richardthelionheart #historypros

beats.say: April 1204. A huge Christian crusader army is attacking one of the richest cities on Earth.
There's just one problem. This army was supposed to be fighting for the Holy Land, around Jerusalem.
And this city isn't in the Holy Land. It's Constantinople, and it's Christian too.
It was the capital of the Byzantine Empire, the Greek-speaking eastern half of the old Roman Empire.
So how does a holy war end up at the wrong city? Short answer: debt. A lot of debt.
And believe it or not, that's not the only crusade that went completely sideways.
Quick background: the Crusades were a series of religious wars from 1096 to the late 1200s. European Christian armies tried to take and hold Jerusalem and the lands around it.
Those lands were ruled by Muslim powers, and they mattered deeply to Christians, Muslims and Jews alike. Today we're skipping the big battles and counting down the weirdest moments.
Number seven. In 1095, Pope Urban the Second called on Europe's knights to march east.
The official armies were told to leave in August 1096, after the harvest was in.
But a preacher called Peter the Hermit didn't feel like waiting.
He preached across France and Germany, and thousands of ordinary people followed him. Farmers, families, and a few knights.
In spring 1096 they set off from Cologne in Germany, months ahead of the real army.
A serious note here. That same year, some crusader bands in Germany attacked Jewish communities along the Rhine river and killed thousands. It's one of the darkest parts of this whole story.
Peter's crowd reached Constantinople that summer. Its emperor, Alexios the First, had asked the West for trained soldiers.
I asked for trained knights. You brought... everyone's cousins?
God's army doesn't wait!
Wonderful. Then God's army can wait over there.
Within days, he ferried them across the water into Asia Minor, where Turkish armies were waiting.
In October, while Peter was back in Constantinople asking for help, his army was ambushed and almost wiped out.
Peter survived. Three years later he did reach Jerusalem, with the official army. He just wasn't in charge anymore.
Number six is famous, but it's a mix of history and legend. In 1212, a German boy called Nicholas started preaching a crusade.
In France, a shepherd boy called Stephen of Cloyes was drawing big crowds too.
Chroniclers say thousands followed Nicholas. Many were young, and many were poor.
They crossed the Alps into Italy. That's the Alps. On foot. To get to a beach.
Accounts say Nicholas promised the sea would dry up for them, so they could walk to the Holy Land.
They reached the port of Genoa in August. They waited. The sea stayed exactly where it was.
Most of them gave up. Some stayed in Italy, and others began the long walk home.
Later legends said many were sold as slaves. Historians can't confirm that. Many also think the crowds were mostly poor wanderers, not just kids.
Number five. In 1219, a crusader army was besieging Damietta, a port city in Egypt.
Egypt's ruler was Sultan al-Kamil, a nephew of Saladin.
Into this war walks Francis of Assisi, an Italian friar who was famous for owning basically nothing.
Francis decided to cross the battle lines, unarmed, and talk to the sultan in person.
Soldiers from the other side picked him up and brought him to the sultan.
You walked here? From that camp? On purpose?
I came to talk, not to fight.
Well. That makes a nice change.
Early accounts say the sultan listened politely, then sent Francis back to the crusader camp safely.
Later storytellers added extra drama. But the meeting itself really happened, and it's still remembered as an early moment of dialogue between the two faiths.
Number four. It's the Third Crusade, around 1191, and two famous enemies are facing off.
On one side is Richard the Lionheart, King of England, a famous fighter.

tag.text: Richard the Lionheart, King of England

beats.say: On the other is Saladin, the sultan who had taken Jerusalem in 1187.

tag.text: Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria

beats.say: They fought big battles. But they also negotiated, mostly through Saladin's brother, al-Adil.
And according to Saladin's adviser, Baha ad-Din, Richard pitched a wild peace plan.
Easy. My sister Joan marries your brother, and they rule Jerusalem together.
You promised me to a man I've never met?
Joan flatly refused, and the plan fell apart.
Then in 1192, Richard fell sick with a fever. Accounts say Saladin sent him fresh fruit, and snow from the mountains to cool his drinks.
Snow. In the Middle Eastern summer. From the guy you're at war with.
In the end, neither man got everything. In September 1192 they signed a three-year truce, and Christian pilgrims could visit Jerusalem again.
Number three is Richard's trip home. A storm wrecked his ship near the top of the Adriatic Sea, so he had to go overland.
The quickest way home went through Austria. Bad news. Its ruler, Duke Leopold, hated Richard.
At the siege of Acre, Richard's men had thrown down Leopold's banner. Leopold never forgot it.
So Richard travelled in disguise. It didn't work. In December 1192 he was recognized near Vienna and arrested.
Remember my banner at Acre, Your Majesty?
Vaguely.
Leopold handed him over to his boss, the German emperor Henry the Sixth, who named a price.
One hundred and fifty thousand marks of silver. Historians put that at two to three times the English crown's yearly income.
England raised it with a giant tax, a quarter of the value of people's income and goods.
There's a famous legend that a minstrel called Blondel found Richard by singing outside castles, until Richard sang back.
Lovely story. But nobody had to search for Richard. The emperor announced the capture in letters. That's how a ransom works.
When Richard's release was agreed, his rival, King Philip of France, warned Richard's brother John, who had plotted to take his throne. A chronicler recorded it: Look to yourself; the devil is loose.

show.text: Look to yourself; the devil is loose.
show.who: King Philip II of France to Prince John, as recorded by Roger of Howden

beats.say: Richard walked free in February 1194.
Number two stars Frederick the Second, the Holy Roman Emperor, who ruled Germany and much of Italy.
He promised to go on crusade. Then he kept not going. When he finally sailed in 1227, he got sick and turned back.
So Pope Gregory the Ninth excommunicated him. That means kicking him out of the Church.
You're excommunicated for not going on crusade!
Fine. I'm going.
You can't go on crusade while you're excommunicated!
He went anyway, in 1228. And instead of fighting, he negotiated with Sultan al-Kamil. Yes, the same sultan Francis met.
In February 1229 they signed the Treaty of Jaffa. Jerusalem went back to Christian rule, without a battle.
It came with a ten-year truce, and Islam's holy sites in Jerusalem stayed in Muslim hands.
Then Frederick held a crown-wearing ceremony in Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre. While still excommunicated.
The deal annoyed plenty of people on both sides. But he got Jerusalem with talks, not swords.

show.title: The Crusade That Hit the Wrong City

beats.say: Number one. In 1201, the leaders of a new crusade hired Venice, a rich sea power in Italy, to ship their army east.
Venice's ruler, the Doge Enrico Dandolo, was blind and probably in his nineties. He was also a very sharp businessman.
The crusaders booked ships for about thirty-three thousand five hundred men. Only about twelve thousand showed up.
So they couldn't pay the bill. They were still short about thirty-four thousand marks.
You owe Venice thirty-four thousand marks.
Could we, maybe, pay you later?
Help me capture a city first. Then we'll talk.
The city was Zara, today Zadar in Croatia. It was a Christian city that had broken away from Venice.
In November 1202 the crusaders captured it. Pope Innocent the Third was furious and excommunicated them.
Then a runaway Byzantine prince, Alexios Angelos, made an offer. Put my father back on the throne in Constantinople, and I'll pay you two hundred thousand marks.
They did it. Then he couldn't pay, and his own people overthrew him. In April 1204 the crusaders stormed Constantinople.
The sack lasted three days. Many people were killed, and churches and palaces were looted. It shocked the whole Christian world.
Venice took famous treasures home, like four bronze horses that still belong to Saint Mark's Basilica in Venice today.
The main crusader army never reached the Holy Land. And it deepened a split between Catholic Christians in the West and Orthodox Christians in the East that lasted for centuries.
Before we go, an honorable mention. King Louis the Ninth of France, later made a saint, invaded Egypt in 1249.
In 1250 his army was beaten, and Louis himself was captured.
His friend Jean de Joinville wrote that Louis agreed to a huge ransom without haggling. The sultan was so impressed, he knocked a chunk off the price.
So: a crusade that left early, a sea that wouldn't part, snow from your enemy, a ransomed king, and the wrong city. Which one was the weirdest? Tell us in the comments.
